clue.text: Arise, then vacate premises, Pep

parts.note: to arise is to get up from bed or a seat
'and' can mean 'and then', as in 'he sat and ate'
to vacate a place is to go from it

explanation.surface: Instructions for a sluggish morning: get out of bed, leave the house, and put some pep into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pep is energy and drive, the same zest the hyphenated phrase names.

clue.text: Cut deeply into left extremity of gum tree

indicators.note: the left end of a written word is its first letter, so take the opening letter of gum

parts.note: the ash is a common tree

explanation.surface: A woodsman carves a deep notch at the base of a gum tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gum tree' reads as one thing, but 'gum' only lends its first letter and 'tree' is ASH.
explanation.definitionFit: A gash is a long deep wound, so as a verb it means to slash something deeply.

clue.text: Measure of duvet, a covering in Rome

parts.note: the tog is the British unit for how warm a duvet or quilt is

explanation.surface: Someone compares a warm duvet rating with what Romans wrapped themselves in.
explanation.walkthrough: TOG is the British rating printed on duvets: the higher the tog, the warmer the quilt.
explanation.definitionFit: The toga was the draped woollen garment worn by citizens of ancient Rome.

clue.text: Mistakenly disheartened, put onto ferry where customs officer seen

indicators.note: done mistakenly, the letters are put together in the wrong order and must be rearranged
with its heart removed the word put keeps only its outside letters

explanation.surface: Someone put on the wrong ferry is gloomy, waiting where the customs officer stands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disheartened' leaves PT from 'put'; with ONTO and FERRY that gives eleven letters for 'Mistakenly' to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A port of entry is the harbour or airport where travellers arriving in a country pass customs.

clue.text: Number: tell us about mathematical concept

indicators.note: about here means moved around, so the letters of tell us are reordered

explanation.surface: A student asks a teacher to explain a numerical idea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges TELL US to make ULLSET, after N for Number.
explanation.definitionFit: In set theory, the set with no members is a basic idea of mathematics.

clue.text: He's mostly got my fancy footwear

indicators.note: fancy as in elaborate or fanciful, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, he is shortened

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all of the word got, so its final letter goes

explanation.surface: Someone admires a stylish pair of shoes another person has acquired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims GOT to GO; 'fancy' rearranges HES, GO and MY.
explanation.definitionFit: A gym shoe is a plimsoll or trainer worn for sport, a kind of footwear.

clue.text: Stain t-shirts etc on the counter

indicators.note: counter as in running against, so the word is read the other way

parts.note: t-shirts and similar garments are tops

explanation.surface: Someone spots a mark on clothing laid out on a shop counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the counter' looks like a shop counter but means read backwards, turning TOPS into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A spot is a small mark or blemish on fabric, just as a stain is.

clue.text: Model embracing latest in latest tech, not analogue communication

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so the other pieces sit within the first

parts.note: to pose is to model for an artist or photographer

indicators.note: the latest letter in a word is its final one

parts.note: IT, information technology, is tech
taken as written

explanation.surface: Amid the latest gadgets, someone still prefers a paper message to digital chat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'latest in latest' means the final letter of the word 'latest'; 'embracing' puts the rest inside the model's stance.
explanation.definitionFit: A sticky paper note is an old-fashioned non-digital way of passing a message.

clue.text: Demand of Heaney, finally, fun poem

parts.note: to demand of someone is to ask them

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the poet's name

parts.note: a lark is a bit of fun

explanation.surface: Someone requests that the poet Seamus Heaney finally write a light-hearted poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Heaney is the Irish poet, which tempts toward his work, but the answer is Shelley's ode.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelley's famous ode addressed to the singing bird is a Romantic poem.

clue.text: Sweeties getting guru's palms messy

indicators.note: messy means jumbled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A spiritual teacher's hands get sticky from handling sweets.
explanation.walkthrough: Here the 's of guru's is kept as a letter S, giving ten letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Sugarplums are small round sugared confections, which British speakers call sweeties.

clue.text: Some striptease artists on the water

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Performers in a strip show are out on a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Asea is an old word meaning at sea, afloat on the ocean.

clue.text: Works — like a magician

definitions.meaning: works means succeeds or achieves the desired effect
read literally, a magician performs an illusion

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for succeeding, and also literally what a conjuror does on stage.

clue.text: Large drinks, ringing 'chink!' cut short as the music starts

indicators.note: ringing means encircling, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: a treble is a triple measure of spirits

indicators.note: cut short means the last letter is removed

parts.note: a chink is a cleft, a narrow crack

explanation.surface: Glasses of drink clink as the band strikes up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ringing' and 'chink' suggest the sound of glasses; in fact 'ringing' is the container and 'chink' a crack.
explanation.definitionFit: The treble clef is the symbol printed at the start of each line of music.

clue.text: Everyman's going to conform — about time! — clothing ultimately not suiting body

parts.note: the setter Everyman saying 'I will' contracts to I'll

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: to fit in is to conform

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so take the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: The setter promises to conform at last, while clothes hang badly on the body.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Everyman's going to' is the setter saying I'LL; 'about' puts T inside FIT IN, and 'ultimately' adds G from clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes that are badly sized do not suit the wearer's body shape.

clue.text: With no starter of duck, utensil wonky — most unfortunate

indicators.note: wonky means crooked, so the letters are rearranged
without its starter the word loses its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone cooking duck finds the kitchen tool bent, an unlucky day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With no starter of' drops D from DUCK to leave UCK; 'wonky' rearranges that with UTENSIL.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of unlucky means having the worst fortune.

clue.text: Easy and fast to welcome Bolshevik spurning banks

indicators.note: to welcome means to take in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Lent is the Christian season of fasting

indicators.note: the banks are the edges, so the word drops its first and last letters

parts.note: Lenin led the Bolshevik revolution

explanation.surface: Fasting is made easier by inviting a revolutionary who rejects banks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spurning banks' sounds political but means dropping a word's first and last letters; 'to welcome' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: Lenient means mild and undemanding, as an easy teacher is.

clue.text: Ear lent, grievously everlasting

indicators.note: grievously means badly, so the letters are put in disorder

explanation.surface: Someone lent a sympathetic ear to grief that seemed endless.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternal means lasting for ever, without end.

clue.text: Endless bother accommodating down-under damned doctor

indicators.note: accommodating means housing, so one piece is placed inside the other
endless means without the final letter

parts.note: a fuss is bother
Aust is an abbreviation for Australia, known as Down Under

explanation.surface: Endless trouble housing a cursed doctor from Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' trims the last letter of the bother word; 'accommodating' houses the Australia abbreviation inside, Australia being known as Down Under.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctor Faustus sold his soul to the devil and was damned, in Marlowe's play.

clue.text: Isolate and largely ignore posho

indicators.note: largely means most of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: to shun is to ignore
a toff is a British slang term for an upper-class person, a posh one

explanation.surface: Someone advises cutting off and mostly snubbing a snob.
explanation.walkthrough: TOFF and posho are both British slang for an upper-class person.
explanation.definitionFit: To shut off something is to cut it off from supply or contact.

clue.text: Recalls Tarantino welcoming having only celebrities

indicators.note: welcoming means holding within, so the answer is a run of letters inside these words

explanation.surface: The director recalls films whose casts were packed with stars.
explanation.definitionFit: An all-star cast is made up entirely of famous performers.

clue.text: Quiet, computer program, quiet

parts.note: an app is a computer program
to ease is to calm or quiet

explanation.surface: Three terse words, like a list of settings on a device.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Quiet' is the definition, a verb meaning to pacify; the second gives EASE.
explanation.definitionFit: To appease is to pacify or calm someone, settling their anger.

clue.text: Choose — like a navvy

definitions.meaning: the idiom means to choose whichever you like
a navvy is a British labourer digging roads, who would pick up a pickaxe

explanation.definitionFit: The idiom invites selection, and read literally describes a labourer grabbing a pickaxe.

clue.text: Film fish: premonition written up

indicators.note: in a down entry, written up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: an omen is a premonition

explanation.surface: A cinema fish senses a warning sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Nemo is the clownfish hero of an animated film about a lost fish.

clue.text: Goodness, Kelvin is a dweeb

parts.note: gee is an exclamation like goodness
K is the symbol for kelvin, the unit of temperature

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise that someone called Kelvin is a nerd.
explanation.definitionFit: Dweeb is slang for a socially awkward, obsessive person, a nerd.

clue.text: Primarily, incenses / raises exasperation / steams?

indicators.note: primarily means firstly, so take the first letter of each following word

explanation.surface: A list of ways that someone is made angry.
explanation.walkthrough: Each phrase also describes anger, so the whole clue serves as definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To anger, incense or exasperate someone is what the verb means, in the third person.

clue.text: A line on a map?

parts.note: not a border or road, but the words printed by the marker on a street map showing where the reader stands

explanation.definitionFit: Public maps label the reader's position with this phrase, a line of text on the map.

clue.text: Removes content of bottle

definitions.meaning: to remove the insides of a fish or building
bottle is British slang for courage

explanation.definitionFit: To gut is to take out the innards; guts also means courage, like British bottle.

clue.text: Dessert wine that's measured with seismometer

parts.note: afters is British slang for dessert, what comes after the main course
hock is German white wine, a British term

explanation.surface: Pudding and a glass of wine after an earthquake.
explanation.walkthrough: AFTERS is British for pudding; HOCK is a British name for German Rhine wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A tremor following a main earthquake is recorded on scientific instruments.
